captions.linkedin:
Here's a one-line signal that beat almost every other anomaly in the 2000s: the year-over-year change in total assets.

Cooper, Gulen & Schill (Journal of Finance, 2008) sorted US equities into deciles by asset growth. Lowest-growth firms beat highest-growth firms across the cross-section for 35 years running.

The metric is one ratio you can compute in a spreadsheet: ΔTotal Assets divided by lagged total assets. Once a year. June formation. Done.

🔹 SIMPLE METRIC, the asset growth ratio is one line of code
🔹 DECILE SORTS, long lowest growth, short highest
🔹 CONTROLS ROBUST, survives size, BM, momentum, accruals
🔹 ANNUAL REBALANCE, June formation with 6-month lag
🔹 LOW TURNOVER, once per year mechanical screening
🔹 UNIVERSALITY, works large-cap, stronger equal-weight

This signal became the I in Fama-French's CMA factor and the I in the Hou-Xue-Zhang q-factor model. Two of the most respected asset pricing models in modern finance both pivot on it.

The magnitude compressed in large-cap post-publication. Still significant globally. Rational q-theory explains it as a cost-of-capital effect, not pure mispricing.

Cooper, Gulen & Schill (2008) Journal of Finance; educational only, not investment advice.
